property_summary: If a caller successfully locks a guess then the caller must have sent exactly 1 ether (so address(c).balance increases by 1 ether and c will accept the guess only when msg.value == 1 ether).
Calling lockInGuess succeeds (does not revert) iff the caller sends exactly 1 ether.
For any call to lockInGuess the call must revert exactly when the supplied value is not 1 ether (i.e., success iff value == 1 ether).
A call to lockInGuess with value != 1 ether always reverts (so reverted == (amount != 1 ether)).
For any caller and any sent amount, lockInGuess reverts exactly when the sent amount is not 1 ether (i.e., it succeeds only for amount == 1 ether).

For any caller who sends exactly 1 ether to lockInGuess, the reference contract accepts the call (does not revert) and records a nonzero guessed block (so lockInGuess succeeds), whereas the mutant requiring 2 ether will reject such a 1-ether call (revert) for some inputs — so try/catch on lockInGuess with value 1 ether distinguishes them.

For any caller and any guess hash, calling lockInGuess with exactly 1 ether succeeds (does not revert) on the reference implementation and records a pending guess (nonzero stored block), while the mutant that requires 2 ether will sometimes revert on the same call; the test fuzzes caller and guess and asserts that lockInGuess(...) with 1 ether always succeeds on the reference.

For any caller address and any guess bytes32, calling lockInGuess with exactly 1 ether never reverts on the reference contract (it accepts and records the guess), whereas the mutant that requires 2 ether will revert for those same inputs (so the call can fail).

For any caller and any guess hash, if the caller sends exactly 1 ether to lockInGuess, the reference C always accepts the call and leaves a nonzero stored block number for that caller (i.e. lockInGuess succeeds and records a pending guess), whereas the mutant requiring 2 ether will revert for some such inputs — so the property: calling lockInGuess with msg.value == 1 ether never reverts on the reference (ok == true) but the mutant can cause ok == false for some inputs.

For any caller and any guess hash, calling lockInGuess(...) with msg.value == 1 ether always succeeds (does not revert) on the reference contract C, but the mutant that changed the required deposit to 2 ether will revert for some such inputs (so a try/catch on a 1 ether call distinguishes them).

For any caller and any guess hash, calling lockInGuess when the caller has no active guess must succeed and set their stored block to a nonzero value without overwriting an existing guess (i.e., a caller cannot replace a prior pending guess); the mutant that removes the 'no existing guess' check allows overwriting a previously-locked guess and block number.

For any caller and any guess hash, once a caller successfully lockInGuess(...) when they had no pending guess, the stored guess and block for that caller remain unchanged by any subsequent lockInGuess(...) call from the same caller before settle() — the mutant that removes the 'no existing guess' check allows overwriting that stored guess/block, violating this invariant.

For any caller who successfully calls lockInGuess with 1 ether, the contract stores a nonzero future block number (strictly greater than the current block) as their guess.block; the mutant that stores block.number (current block) can violate this by recording a block that is not strictly in the future.

After a successful lockInGuess call paying 1 ether, the reference contract always records a stored block strictly greater than the block at which lockInGuess was executed (i.e., a future block), whereas the mutant can record the current block (not strictly greater), violating this rule for some inputs.

After any successful lockInGuess call paying exactly 1 ether, the reference contract always records a stored block number strictly greater than the block at which lockInGuess executed (a future block); the mutant that stores block.number can record a non-future block (equal to the current block), violating this rule for some inputs.

For any caller who successfully calls lockInGuess paying exactly 1 ether, the stored block number for that caller is nonzero and strictly greater than zero (i.e., the reference always stores a nonzero/future-semantics marker while the mutant may store the current block which is still nonzero but differs in being equal to block.number); we assert that after calling lockInGuess the stored block is nonzero (the reference sets it to block.number+1 so it's nonzero) — the mutant can still set nonzero though, so instead we assert that immediately after lockInGuess, trying to settle in the same block must revert (because reference stored a future block so settle requires block.number>stored and will revert), while the mutant that stores block.number would allow settle in the same block (not require strictly greater) — thus the general rule: after lockInGuess, calling settle in the same block reverts on the reference for all inputs, but the mutant may not revert for some inputs.

After a successful lockInGuess with exactly 1 ether, attempting to call settle in the SAME block must NOT pay out (i.e., address(c).balance remains unchanged) for the reference contract because it records a future block to check blockhash; the mutant that stores the current block can allow a payout in the same block for some guesses and thus reduce contract balance — the rule: calling settle in the same block after lockInGuess never decreases the contract balance in the reference, but the mutant can decrease it for some inputs.

For any caller who successfully calls lockInGuess with 1 ether, the reference contract stores the submitted guess bytes32 in its public mapping (so reading guesses[caller].guess returns the same hash after the call); the mutant clears the guess immediately and thus for some inputs (any caller) the stored guess is zero, violating this rule.

For any caller who successfully calls lockInGuess with exactly 1 ether, the contract stores the provided bytes32 hash in the public mapping guesses[caller].guess (non-zero when the provided hash is non-zero); the mutant that clears the guess breaks this by leaving the stored guess zero for some inputs.

For any caller who successfully calls lockInGuess with exactly 1 ether and a nonzero bytes32 guess, the reference contract stores that guess in its public mapping so reading guesses[caller].guess returns the same nonzero value after the call; the mutant that clears the guess breaks this by leaving the stored guess equal to zero for such inputs.

For any caller who calls lockInGuess with exactly 1 ether, the reference contract persists the provided bytes32 guess in the public mapping guesses[caller].guess (so reading it after the call returns the same value); the mutant immediately clears the stored guess breaking this rule for inputs where the provided guess is nonzero.

For any caller who successfully calls lockInGuess with exactly 1 ether, the reference contract persists the provided bytes32 guess in its public mapping so reading guesses[caller].guess after the call equals the provided guess; the mutant that clears the guess breaks this (stored guess becomes zero for some inputs).

For any caller and any input hash, after a successful lockInGuess call the contract's stored guess equals the provided hash (i.e. guesses[msg.sender].guess == hash); the mutant that XORs the hash with 1 breaks this by storing a different value for some hashes.

For every caller and every submitted hash, after lockInGuess completes the stored guess equals the submitted hash (so reading the public getter returns the same bytes32); the mutant that XORs the hash with 1 will for some fuzzed hash values cause the stored guess to differ, violating this equality.

For any caller and any submitted hash, calling lockInGuess stores a guess value whose XOR with the submitted hash is either 0 or 1; the reference always stores the exact hash (XOR = 0) while the mutant flips the low bit (XOR = 1) for some inputs, so asserting the XOR equals 0 is universally true for the reference and fails for the mutant on some input.

For any caller and any submitted bytes32 hash, after a successful lockInGuess call the stored guess's low bit equals the low bit of the submitted hash (i.e. (stored ^ hash) & 1 == 0) — the mutant flips that low bit for some inputs so this property is violated.

For every caller and any submitted bytes32 hash, after a successful lockInGuess the stored guess equals either the submitted hash or the submitted hash XOR bytes32(uint256(1)) — the reference always stores exactly the submitted hash, while the mutant stores hash ^ 1 for some inputs, thus violating the 'stored guess equals submitted hash or its XOR-with-1 is zero' rule (so asserting that either stored==hash or stored==hash^1 holds will pass for reference for all inputs but be falsified by the mutant for some inputs).

Reference requires settle() to be callable only in a later block than the stored guess block (block.number > storedBlock) so callers cannot settle in the same block that was recorded; the mutant allowing >= permits settle in the same block which lets blockhash return 0 and still clear state/ether differently — the test asserts that if settle is called in the same block as lockInGuess then the correct contract will revert (settle not allowed) while the mutant will allow the call to proceed and clear the guess (making address(c).balance change).

For any caller who locked a guess, calling settle in the same block as lockInGuess is disallowed by the correct contract (settle must not succeed in that block), whereas the mutant allowing >= permits settle to run in the same block and will clear the guess and possibly change contract balance; thus the invariant is: if settle is invoked in the same block as the stored guess block then settle must revert (or not succeed) on the reference but the mutant may succeed and change address(c).balance.

For every caller who has a locked guess, calling settle for that caller in any block strictly greater than the recorded guess block does not clear the guess if blockhash of the recorded block is zero (i.e., when answer==0), but the mutant can clear the guess (and thus change address(c).balance) by allowing settle in the same block when blockhash is zero; the reference always preserves funds/state when answer==0 while the mutant may clear state/funds for some inputs.

For any caller who has locked a guess, calling settle in the same block as the stored guess block must be disallowed (reference reverts / does not clear state), whereas the mutant allowing '>=' permits settle to succeed in that same block and thus can clear the stored guess and change address(c).balance for some inputs.

For any caller who locked a guess, if settle() is invoked in the same block as the stored guess block then on the correct contract settle() is disallowed (reverts) whereas the mutant allowing '>=' permits settle() to run and clear the stored guess (observable as address(c).balance changing) for some inputs.

For any caller who wins (their guess equals the blockhash and blockhash != 0) the reference contract always clears their stored guess.block (so they cannot repeatedly claim) even if the recipient's transfer fails; the mutant clears the storage only after a successful transfer, so if the transfer reverts the storage remains set and behavior differs.

For every call to settle by a player that previously locked a guess, the reference contract always clears that player’s stored guess.block (so they cannot claim again) regardless of whether the payout transfer succeeds or reverts; the mutant only clears the stored block after a successful transfer, so if the transfer reverts the stored block remains set and the property is violated.

For any caller who previously locked a guess and then calls settle after the guess block has passed, the reference contract always clears that caller's stored guesses[caller].block (so a subsequent settle call will not find a pending guess); the mutant leaves guesses[caller].block non-zero if the payout transfer to the caller reverts, violating this invariant for callers whose receive() reverts.

For any admissible caller who locked a guess and then calls settle after the guessed block, the reference C always clears guesses[caller].block (so a subsequent settle will revert for lack of a pending guess); the mutant fails to clear guesses[caller].block if the payout transfer to the caller reverts, leaving the mapping nonzero and breaking that invariant.

For any caller who locked a guess and later calls settle after the guessed block, the reference contract always resets guesses[caller].block to 0 by the time settle returns (so a subsequent call to settle will revert for lack of a pending guess); the mutant can leave guesses[caller].block nonzero if the recipient's payable fallback reverts during transfer, violating this invariant.

For any caller who locked a guess and then calls settle after the target block, the reference contract only pays out 2 ether when the stored guess equals the blockhash (and thus never increases contract balance loss for matching guesses), whereas the mutant pays out when the stored guess differs from the blockhash — so the invariant is: after settle, address(c).balance is decreased by 2 ether iff the stored guess equaled the blockhash (reference); the mutant instead decreases balance when they differed.

For any caller who locked a guess for block N, the reference contract compares the stored guess to blockhash(N) when settle() is called (so settling can only win if guess == blockhash(N)); the mutant instead compares to blockhash(N-1), so there exist inputs (a chosen lockInGuess block and timing) where reference's comparison result (and thus payout / observable equality of the compared value) differs from the mutant.

For any address that locked a guess for block N, calling settle after block N causes the contract to compare the stored guess to blockhash(N) (reference) — i.e., the payout/observable result depends on blockhash(N) — whereas the mutant compares to blockhash(N-1), so there exist choices of lock block and timing where the reference's compare outcome (and thus whether settle pays) differs from the mutant.

For any actor who locked a guess, when settle() is called the correct contract always compares the stored guess to blockhash(lockedBlock) (so the returned compared value equals blockhash(lockedBlock)), whereas the mutant compares to blockhash(lockedBlock-1) and thus for some choices of lockedBlock and current block the value read (and whether the guess matches it) differs — we assert that settle()'s observed payout outcome for the locker equals whether their stored guess equals blockhash(lockedBlock) using the contract's behavior.

For any actor who locked a guess, calling settle after the locked block will result in the contract comparing the stored guess to the blockhash of the locked block (so whether settle pays equals (storedGuess == blockhash(lockedBlock))); the mutant that reads blockhash(lockedBlock-1) violates this for some choices of lockedBlock/current block.

For any caller who locked a guess for block N, calling settle after block N always makes the reference contract compare the stored guess to blockhash(N) (so the payout/observable match equals (storedGuess == blockhash(N))); the mutant that reads blockhash(N-1) can produce a different settle outcome for some choices of N and timing.
